connections.why: Relative masses and formulae are the basis of the mole and reacting quantities
Titration calculations apply moles to acid–base and redox reactions
Electron configuration and bonding explain periodic trends in properties
Covalent bonding and electron movement underpin organic structures and mechanisms
Group reactivity is studied through redox and displacement reactions
Hess-cycle enthalpies extend into lattice enthalpy, entropy and free energy
Qualitative collision and equilibrium ideas become rate equations and Kc
Acid–base chemistry is quantified through Ka, pH and buffer calculations
Oxidation numbers and half-equations lead into electrode potentials
The d-block extends periodic patterns into complex-ion chemistry
Transition-metal redox couples are explained by electrode potentials
Bonding in alkenes contrasts with the delocalised stability of benzene
Oxidising alcohols produces the aldehydes and ketones studied later
Further oxidation of carbonyls gives carboxylic acids and their derivatives
Ester and amide linkages form the basis of condensation polymers
Amino acids condense via peptide bonds into polyamide proteins
IR and MS combine with NMR and chromatography for full structure determination
Mechanisms and functional-group reactions are combined in multi-step synthesis
Weak-acid behaviour explains the acidity of carboxylic acids
Titration technique is a core practical applying acid–base chemistry
Rate experiments and their analysis are assessed in written practical questions
d-orbital splitting explains the colour and bonding of complex ions
